title: Application-contract-driven maintenance slicer for Dedicated fleets
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
Design and implement a maintenance scheduler that slices fleet capacity by application-level throughput contracts ("throughput contracts") so maintenance windows (upgrades/drains/reboots) are executed with explicit guarantees to each contract. This ticket covers design, runtime changes, autoscaler integration, operator console controls, and rollout plan for Dedicated customers.

Motivation:
Customers on Dedicated require predictable throughput during maintenance. Current approach (fleet-wide drains) causes transient throughput loss and customer-visible latency spikes. By carving the fleet into maintenance slices aligned with application contracts and orchestration policies (staggered drains, reserved slots, emergency kill switch), we can offer customers explicit maintenance SLOs and reduce incidents during upgrades.

Goals / Success criteria:
- Implement maintenance-slicing controller that reserves a fraction of capacity per contract and schedules maintenance waves without violating declared throughput guarantees.
- Maintenance operations should keep observed throughput drop <= 5% for a contract and p99 latency regression <= 3% for critical routes during scheduled windows.
- Allow operators and tenants to opt into "high-availability maintenance" with smaller slice sizes and more aggressive prewarming.
- Integrate with autoscaler so reserved-slice capacity is respected and burst lanes are used only when allowed by policy.

High-level design:
1) Throughput contracts: a small API/CRD where tenant/team declares (max sustained QPS, burst headroom, SLO class). These map to slice quotas (CPU/GPU slots, ephemeral slot tokens).
2) Maintenance slicer: controller that computes maintenance waves by slicing hosts into maintenance buckets that minimize cross-contract interference. The slicer schedules drains in buckets with warming preconditions (KV cache warm, model cache present) and enforces minimum live-slice capacity.
3) Autoscaler integration: the cluster autoscaler must treat reserved slice capacity as non-evictable for the duration of the maintenance window; we introduce a reservation token the autoscaler recognizes to prevent scale-in that would violate commitments.
4) Graceful kill switch & emergency fallback: operator-facing API to pause maintenance, trigger fallback routing to compatible model variants, or temporarily allocate burst capacity from global pool.
5) Console & observability: new per-contract dashboards (expected vs observed throughput, latency delta, maintenance wave timeline), alerts when maintenance risks breaching contract.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Week 1-2: Spec and API (Confluence doc + public API schema) + proto for reservation token.
- Week 3-4: Scheduler prototype in staging that reads declared contracts and proposes maintenance waves (dry-run mode).
- Week 5: KV/model cache prewarm hooks + hook into existing drain process.
- Week 6-7: Autoscaler changes to honor reservation tokens and new unit tests.
- Week 8: Canary rollout on low-traffic Dedicated cluster; collect metrics.
- Week 9-10: Operator console UI and alerting, docs, runbook, and full rollout.

Rollout & Safety:
- Start in dry-run (no actual drains) for 2 weeks to verify schedule decisions and ensure no API regressions.
- Canary run in non-production Dedicated fleet with synthetic traffic that simulates contract mixes. Thresholds: throughput drop <= 5% and p99 latency <= 3%.
- Gradual ramp to production with human-in-loop approvals for the first three maintenance windows.

Metrics to observe:
- Per-contract sustained QPS (expected vs actual)
- Latency p50/p90/p99 delta during maintenance windows
- Number of fallback events (emergency kill switch)
- Autoscaler scale-ins blocked by reservation tokens

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Contract granularity: allocate by route, tenant, or service? (We recommend route-level contracts for fine-grained cost attribution but start with tenant-level.)
- Reservation accounting: how to bill reserved tokens? Upfront commit vs consumption-based? We propose deferring billing changes until after operational validation.
- Complexity vs predictability: the slicer adds scheduler complexity; consider offering as an opt-in advanced capability for customers with SLO requirements.

Related artifacts and links:
- Spec (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/Throughput+Contract+Spec (draft)
- Prototype scheduler repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/dedicated-maintenance-slicer/pull/12
- Staging dashboard (Grafana): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/dedicated/maintenance-slicer-staging

Runbook snippets (for on-call):
- If contract throughput falls >10% for >2 minutes: pause maintenance wave, trigger prewarm for affected contract slices, and notify on-call.
- If p99 latency regression > 5%: abort wave and run emergency fallback to model variant with lower memory footprint.

Risks:
- Incorrect reservation accounting may reduce overall cluster efficiency. Mitigation: limit initial reservation to small fraction (10-15%) and monitor cluster utilization.
- Bugs in autoscaler integration could cause unexpected scale-in blocking; mitigate with feature flags and simulated scale events in staging.

Next steps:
- Finalize API schema and attach to this ticket.
- Assign eng owners for autoscaler and scheduler components.
- Kick off prototype implementation in Week 3.
